title: Systematic Personnel Training as the Foundation for Biological Sovereignty in African Countries: Experience in Implementing Rospotrebnadzor Educational Programs for Specialists from the Republic of Burundi (2023–2025)
abstract: The aim of the study was to describe the experience in introduction, systematization and thematic analysis of the implemented programs of the Rospotrebnadzor for specialists of the Republic of Burundi (2023–2025) in the field of laboratory diagnostics, epidemiological monitoring and biosafety as part of the strategy to strengthen the biological sovereignty of African states. Materials and methods. The study is based on the analysis of reporting documents and educational materials from 15 advanced training courses and field exercises conducted for the staff of the National Institute of Public Health of Burundi (INSP) in 2023–2025. The training was delivered in English using adapted educational programs. Descriptive statistics and content analysis of course topics were employed. Results and discussion. During the reporting period, 16 educational events were conducted, over 130 specialists were trained. The programs covered such key areas as: general laboratory practice and biosafety (PBA of II–IV pathogenicity groups), molecular diagnostics (including third-generation sequencing on the MinION platform and LAMP), serological screening (ELISA diagnostics of natural-focal and hepatotropic infections), bacteriology of food-borne infections, zoological and entomological surveillance, as well as specific pathology (HIV infection, mpox). In October 2024, field exercises using a mobile laboratory for indication and monitoring of particularly dangerous infections (MLIM) were carried out. It is shown that systemic transfer of competencies, rather than one-time equipment supplies, forms the basis for autonomous response to biological threats. The implemented programs have confirmed the effectiveness of systematic approach to personnel training as a tool for strengthening the national laboratory network. The coverage of modern diagnostic methods meets the current needs of the republic. The developed educational modules have potential for duplication in other developing African countries.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在描述2023–2025年间俄罗斯联邦国家消费者权益保护和公共健康监督局(Rospotrebnadzor)为布隆迪共和国专业人员实施的实验室诊断、流行病学监测和生物安全项目在引入、系统化和主题分析方面的经验,作为加强非洲国家生物主权战略的一部分。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究基于对2023–2025年间为布隆迪共和国国家公共卫生研究所(INSP)工作人员开展的15项高级培训课程和现场演练的报告文件和教学材料的分析。
elements_zh.methods: 项目涵盖的关键领域包括:一般实验室操作与生物安全(II–IV类病原体的PBA)、分子诊断(包括MinION平台上的第三代测序和LAMP技术)、血清学筛查(自然疫源性和肝炎相关感染的ELISA诊断)、食源性感染的细菌学、动物学和昆虫学监测,以及特定病理(HIV感染,猴痘)。2024年10月,使用移动实验室(MLIM)进行了针对特别危险感染的现场演练。
elements_zh.main_results: 在报告期间,共举办了16次教育活动,培训了超过130名专业人员。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究表明,系统性地转移专业技能,而非一次性设备供应,是自主应对生物威胁的基础。所实施的项目证实了系统性人员培训方法在加强国家实验室网络方面的有效性。现代诊断方法的覆盖范围满足了共和国当前的需求。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 所开发的教学模块在其他发展中国家具有复制潜力。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究基于对报告文件和教学材料的分析,可能无法完全反映培训项目的实际效果。样本量仅限于布隆迪共和国国家公共卫生研究所(INSP)的工作人员。

title: Analysis of immediate upstream gene regions in orthopoxvirus genomes through the use of DNA Duplex Stability and explainable machine learning
abstract: Orthopoxviruses are double-stranded DNA viruses with a temporally regulated gene expression program divided into early, intermediate, and late stages. Although many temporal gene functions are known, the promoter features that distinguish expression program require more precise characterization. Here, we employed an explainable machine learning approach to classify upstream gene regions as either early or non-early using the DNA Duplex Stability (DDS) as a numerical representation. We trained a Random Forest model on NCBI orthopoxvirus genomes and evaluated it using a public transcriptomic dataset of the agent Orthopoxvirus monkeypox virus (MPXV). To determine how individual features contributed to model predictions, we employed SHAP explainable Artificial Intelligence tool. Our results show that the region from -10 to -1 relative to the start codon is highly informative for class distinction. We found that the TAAAT-like motif at position -3 is a strong predictor of the non-early class, even in sequences originally labeled as early, providing insights into its multi-stage functionality. These findings provide an interpretable framework for identifying CDS proximal regions features linked to the temporal regulation of orthopoxvirus genes. This approach may support regulatory region annotation in newly sequenced genomes and help prioritize promoter variants affecting viral gene expression.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在表征区分正痘病毒时间调控基因表达程序的启动子特征,特别是关注早期和非早期阶段。该研究的动机源于对这些调控机制更精确理解的需求。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究采用了一种可解释的机器学习方法,将正痘病毒 基因组的上游基因区域分类为早期或非早期。它使用DNA双链稳定性(DDS)作为数值表示,并通过猴痘病毒(MPXV)的公共转录组数据集评估了该模型。
elements_zh.methods: 研究人员使用NCBI上的正痘病毒 基因组数据训练了一个随机森林模型,并利用SHAP可解释人工智能工具来确定单个特征如何影响模型预测。他们专注于将上游基因区域的DNA双链稳定性(DDS)作为数值表示。
elements_zh.main_results: 结果显示,相对于起始密码子,从-10到-1的区域对于区分早期和非早期类别具有高度信息性。在位置-3处的TAAAT样基序被鉴定为预测非早期类别的强指标,即使在最初标记为早期的序列中也是如此。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 这些发现为识别与正痘病毒基因时间调控相关的编码序列(CDS)邻近区域特征提供了一个可解释的框架,为理解其多阶段功能提供了新的见解。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果可能支持对新测序的基因组的调控区域注释,并有助于优先考虑影响病毒基因表达的启动子变体,这可能对理解与管理猴痘疾病具有重要意义。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究仅限于分析公共转录组数据集,未包括对模型预测的实验验证。由于依赖计算方法而没有直接的生物学测试,证据强度中等。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to characterize the promoter features that distinguish the temporally regulated gene expression program of orthopoxviruses, particularly focusing on the early and non-early stages. The research was motivated by the need for more precise understanding of these regulatory mechanisms.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: The study employed an explainable machine learning approach to classify upstream gene regions of orthopoxvirus genomes as early or non-early. It used the DNA Duplex Stability (DDS) as a numerical representation and evaluated the model using a public transcriptomic dataset of the monkeypox virus (MPXV).
analysis_en.methods: The researchers trained a Random Forest model on NCBI orthopoxvirus genomes and utilized the SHAP explainable AI tool to determine how individual features contributed to model predictions. They focused on the DNA Duplex Stability (DDS) as a numerical representation of upstream gene regions.
analysis_en.main_results: The results showed that the region from -10 to -1 relative to the start codon is highly informative for distinguishing between early and non-early classes. The TAAAT-like motif at position -3 was identified as a strong predictor of the non-early class, even in sequences originally labeled as early.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings provide an interpretable framework for identifying features in the coding sequence (CDS) proximal regions linked to the temporal regulation of orthopoxvirus genes, offering novel insights into their multi-stage functionality.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results may support regulatory region annotation in newly sequenced genomes and help prioritize promoter variants that affect viral gene expression, which could have implications for understanding and managing mpox disease.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to the analysis of a public transcriptomic dataset and does not include experimental validation of the model's predictions. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the reliance on computational methods without direct biological testing.

title_zh: 通过DNA双链稳定性分析和可解释机器学习对正痘病毒 基因组中立即上游基因区域进行分析
source_body_en: Orthopoxviruses are double-stranded DNA viruses with a temporally regulated gene expression program divided into early, intermediate, and late stages. Although many temporal gene functions are known, the promoter features that distinguish expression program require more precise characterization. Here, we employed an explainable machine learning approach to classify upstream gene regions as either early or non-early using the DNA Duplex Stability (DDS) as a numerical representation. We trained a Random Forest model on NCBI orthopoxvirus genomes and evaluated it using a public transcriptomic dataset of the agent Orthopoxvirus monkeypox virus (MPXV). To determine how individual features contributed to model predictions, we employed SHAP explainable Artificial Intelligence tool. Our results show that the region from -10 to -1 relative to the start codon is highly informative for class distinction. We found that the TAAAT-like motif at position -3 is a strong predictor of the non-early class, even in sequences originally labeled as early, providing insights into its multi-stage functionality. These findings provide an interpretable framework for identifying CDS proximal regions features linked to the temporal regulation of orthopoxvirus genes. This approach may support regulatory region annotation in newly sequenced genomes and help prioritize promoter variants affecting viral gene expression.
abstract_zh: 正痘病毒是具有时间调控基因表达程序的双链DNA病毒,该程序分为早期、中期和晚期阶段。尽管许多时间基因功能已被了解,但区分表达程序的启动子特征仍需更精确的表征。在此研究中,我们采用了一种可解释的机器学习方法,利用DNA双链稳定性(DDS)作为数值表示,将上游基因区域分类为早期或非早期。我们使用NCBI上的正痘病毒 基因组数据训练了一个随机森林模型,并通过猴痘病毒(MPXV)的公共转录组数据集评估了该模型。为了确定单个特征如何影响模型预测,我们采用了SHAP可解释人工智能工具。我们的结果显示,相对于起始密码子,从-10到-1的区域对于类别区分具有高度信息性。我们发现,在位置-3处的TAAAT样基序是预测非早期类别的强指标,即使在最初标记为早期的序列中也是如此,这为理解其多阶段功能提供了见解。这些发现为识别与正痘病毒基因时间调控相关的编码序列(CDS)邻近区域特征提供了一个可解释的框架。这种方法可能支持对新测序的基因组的调控区域注释,并有助于优先考虑影响病毒基因表达的启动子变体。

full_text: Monkeypox Related Keratouveitis: A Case Report Published 2026 - 44th Congress of the ESCRS Reference: POCOR019 | Type: Case Report | DOI: 10.82333/dcn1-x864 Authors: Dr Assaf Almalki* 1 , Dr Majed Alsubaie 1 , Dr Talal Aljudi 1 1Ophthalmology,Dhahran Eye Specialist Hospital,Dhahran,Saudi Arabia Purpose The purpose of this case report is to present the clinical course and management of a 34-year-old male with Monkeypox-related keratitis in the right eye. Aiming to highlight therapeutic interventions and initial outcomes of a patient with Monkeypox-related keratouveitis. Setting This case was presented and managed at Dhahran Eye Specialist Hospital (DESH). The patient presented to the emergency room (ER) with severe sub-acute ocular symptoms, including swelling, pain, photophobia, and decreased vision. Prior to his presentation, the patient was diagnosed with Monkeypox with skin manifestations in another hospital. Report of case A 34-year-old male with a history of Monkeypox 2 months prior to presenting to the ER with a complaint of right eye swelling, pain, redness, tearing, photophobia, and decrease of VA. The patient had visited other centers with limited improvement. His VA was CF2ft, and IOP of 28, the SLE showed moderate conjunctival injection, corneal haze, inferior crescent shaped stromal infiltrate with CED of 2* 4 mm, the anterior chamber had +2 mixed cells with flare, no clear view to the iris or fundus. B-scan revealed a flat retina, no choroidal thickening, and quiet posterior segment. Our impression was Herpetic versus Monkeypox-related Keratouveitis. Oral Valacyclovir, Topical Cyclopentolate, Moxifloxacin, and Dorzolamide\Timolol were started, with close F/U. During subsequent visits, the patient had reported improvement, however, the clinical picture remained the same initially. 1 month later, CED was healed and the vision improved to 20\400 and 20\200. Cyclopentolate was switched to Cyclosporine at one point, and the patient was stabilized by the 3-month mark. Awaiting full stabilization to consider PKP. Conclusion/Take home message This case emphasises the importance of detailed history taking in ocular settings, leading to early recognition and management. It also highlights the multimodal treatment methods of combining systemic and topical medications. Close follow-up role is demonstrated in this case, as it allowed adaptive therapy and management of complications. Consideration of surgical intervention for better visual potential.

title_original: Monkeypox Related Keratouveitis: A Case Report

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to highlight therapeutic interventions and initial outcomes of a patient with Monkeypox-related keratouveitis.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This is a case report of a 34-year-old male with Monkeypox-related keratitis in the right eye, presented and managed at Dhahran Eye Specialist Hospital. The patient had a history of Monkeypox with skin manifestations 2 months prior to presenting with ocular symptoms.
analysis.methods: The patient was treated with oral Valacyclovir, topical Cyclopentolate, Moxifloxacin, and Dorzolamide\Timolol, with close follow-up. The clinical course was monitored through subsequent visits to assess improvement and stabilization.
analysis.main_results: The patient had severe sub-acute ocular symptoms, including swelling, pain, photophobia, and decreased vision. His VA was CF2ft, and IOP was 28. The SLE showed moderate conjunctival injection, corneal haze, inferior crescent shaped stromal infiltrate with CED of 2* 4 mm, and +2 mixed cells with flare. B-scan revealed a flat retina, no choroidal thickening, and quiet posterior segment. The patient reported improvement, but the clinical picture remained the same initially. One month later, CED was healed, and vision improved to 20\400 and 20\200. Cyclopentolate was switched to Cyclosporine, and the patient was stabilized by the 3-month mark.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as emphasizing the importance of detailed history taking in ocular settings for early recognition and management of Monkeypox-related keratouveitis. They also highlighted the multimodal treatment methods of combining systemic and topical medications.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the need for vigilance in ocular settings when assessing patients with a history of Monkeypox, as well as the potential for multimodal treatment approaches in managing such cases.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its case report design, which provides limited generalizability. However, the evidence is strong as it is based on direct clinical observations and follow-up.

analysis.summary_en: This case report describes a 34-year-old male with Monkeypox-related keratouveitis who presented with severe ocular symptoms, including swelling, pain, photophobia, and decreased vision. The patient had a prior diagnosis of Monkeypox with skin manifestations. Clinical findings included corneal haze, stromal infiltrate, and mixed cells in the anterior chamber. The patient was treated with a combination of systemic and topical medications, including Valacyclovir, Cyclopentolate, Moxifloxacin, and Dorzolamide\Timolol. His vision improved over time, and he was stabilized by the 3-month mark. The authors emphasize the importance of detailed history taking in ocular settings for early recognition and management of Monkeypox-related keratouveitis, as well as the value of multimodal treatment approaches. The study highlights the need for close follow-up and the potential for surgical intervention to improve visual outcomes. The evidence is strong due to direct clinical observations, but the case report design limits generalizability.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在突出猴痘相关角膜内炎患者的治疗干预和初步结果。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究为一个病例报告,描述一名34岁男性患者因右眼猴痘相关角膜炎就诊并接受管理的情况。该患者在出现眼部症状前2个月曾因猴痘伴有皮肤表现而就诊。
elements_zh.methods: 患者接受了口服伐昔洛韦、局部环戊醇、莫西沙星和多佐胺/噻吗洛尔治疗,并进行了密切随访。通过后续就诊监测临床过程,以评估病情改善和稳定情况。
elements_zh.main_results: 患者出现了严重的亚急性眼部症状,包括肿胀、疼痛、畏光和视力下降。其视力为CF2ft,眼内压为28 mmHg。前房角膜后弹力层(SLE)显示中度结膜充血、角膜雾状混浊、下部新月形基质浸润,浸润范围为2*4 mm,前房中有+2级混合细胞伴房水闪辉。B超显示视网膜平坦,无脉络膜增厚,后段安静。患者报告症状有所改善,但初始临床表现未发生变化。一个月后,浸润范围已愈合,视力改善至20/400和20/200。环戊醇被更换为环孢素,患者在3个月时病情稳定。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为强调在眼科环境中详细询问病史对于早期识别和管理猴痘相关角膜内炎的重要性。他们还突出了多模式治疗方法,即结合全身和局部药物治疗。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以为在评估有猴痘病史的患者时,在眼科环境中保持警惕提供依据,同时也可以为管理此类病例的多模式治疗方法提供参考。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究受限于其病例报告设计,因此其推广性有限。然而,证据是强有力的,因为它基于直接的临床观察和随访。

title: Analysis of Mpox intervention measures in presence of environmental transmission pathway using data from DRC
abstract: This paper develops a mathematical model for Mpox transmission dynamics accounting for disease transmission through interpersonal contact as well as from microbes infested environment. The endemic equilibrium of the model was evaluated for two cases. (1) When it is assumed that the microbes in the environment play no role in the spread of the disease, and it was shown that the endemic equilibrium is unique, exists when R 0 is greater than unity, and is globally asymptotically stable. (2) For the case when environmental microbes concentration plays a role in disease transmission, the model was shown to possibly exhibit backward bifurcation at R 0 . This indicates that lowering R 0 below 1 may not eliminate Mpox when the disease is already endemic, due to the stable endemic equilibrium. Numerical results, based on outbreak data from the DRC indicate that; (1) increased interpersonal contact has the potential of making the disease worse, (2) high isolation rate and accelerated recovery of infected individuals through any possible intervention can easily contain the disease. The results further show that environmental contamination does not substantially influence disease transmission rates. More still, it is observed that implementation of influential mitigation measures results in lower and delayed peaks of the number of infected. This is essential for healthcare systems to prepare for more emergency cases and isolation facilities when needed most especially in under resourced communities or countries. Our findings highlight the need for comprehensive interventions addressing both behavioural and environmental factors, especially in environments with limited resources.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本文开发了一个数学模型,用于分析猴痘 传播动态,考虑了通过人际接触以及微生物污染环境传播疾病的影响。本研究旨在了解环境传播在猴痘传播中的作用以及干预措施的有效性。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究评估了两种情况下数学模型的地方性平衡:(1)当环境微生物在疾病 传播 中没有发挥作用时,以及(2)当它们确实发挥作用时。该模型基于 DRC 的 暴发 数据。
elements_zh.methods: 该模型针对两种情况进行了评估:(1) 当环境微生物在疾病 传播 中没有发挥作用时,以及 (2) 当它们确实发挥作用时。结果基于刚果民主共和国的 暴发 数据。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: This paper develops a mathematical model for Mpox transmission dynamics accounting for disease transmission through interpersonal contact as well as from microbes infested environment. The study aimed to understand the role of environmental transmission in Mpox spread and the effectiveness of intervention measures.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: The study evaluated the endemic equilibrium of a mathematical model for two cases: (1) when environmental microbes play no role in disease transmission, and (2) when they do play a role. The model was based on outbreak data from the DRC.
analysis_en.methods: The model was evaluated for two cases: (1) when environmental microbes play no role in disease transmission, and (2) when they do play a role. The results were based on outbreak data from the DRC.
analysis_en.main_results: Numerical results based on outbreak data from the DRC indicate that increased interpersonal contact has the potential of making the disease worse, and high isolation rate and accelerated recovery of infected individuals through any possible intervention can easily contain the disease. Environmental contamination does not substantially influence disease transmission rates.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The results suggest that lowering R 0 below 1 may not eliminate Mpox when the disease is already endemic, due to the stable endemic equilibrium. The findings highlight the need for comprehensive interventions addressing both behavioural and environmental factors, especially in environments with limited resources.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform healthcare systems to prepare for more emergency cases and isolation facilities when needed, especially in under resourced communities or countries. Comprehensive interventions are needed to effectively manage Mpox outbreaks.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the use of a mathematical model and the reliance on outbreak data from the DRC.

title_zh: 在DRC数据支持下分析猴痘干预措施在存在环境传播途径中的情况
source_body_en: This paper develops a mathematical model for Mpox transmission dynamics accounting for disease transmission through interpersonal contact as well as from microbes infested environment. The endemic equilibrium of the model was evaluated for two cases. (1) When it is assumed that the microbes in the environment play no role in the spread of the disease, and it was shown that the endemic equilibrium is unique, exists when R 0 is greater than unity, and is globally asymptotically stable. (2) For the case when environmental microbes concentration plays a role in disease transmission, the model was shown to possibly exhibit backward bifurcation at R 0 . This indicates that lowering R 0 below 1 may not eliminate Mpox when the disease is already endemic, due to the stable endemic equilibrium. Numerical results, based on outbreak data from the DRC indicate that; (1) increased interpersonal contact has the potential of making the disease worse, (2) high isolation rate and accelerated recovery of infected individuals through any possible intervention can easily contain the disease. The results further show that environmental contamination does not substantially influence disease transmission rates. More still, it is observed that implementation of influential mitigation measures results in lower and delayed peaks of the number of infected. This is essential for healthcare systems to prepare for more emergency cases and isolation facilities when needed most especially in under resourced communities or countries. Our findings highlight the need for comprehensive interventions addressing both behavioural and environmental factors, especially in environments with limited resources.
abstract_zh: 本文开发了一个 猴痘 传播 动态数学模型,用于解释通过人际接触以及微生物感染环境产生的疾病 传播。对两个病例的模型的地方性平衡进行了评估。(1) 假设环境中的微生物对疾病的传播没有作用,并且证明地方病平衡是唯一的,当R 0 大于1时存在,并且全局渐近稳定。(2) 对于环境微生物浓度在疾病传播中起作用的情况,模型被证明可能在R 0 处表现出向后分岔。这表明,当疾病已经流行时,由于稳定​​的流行平衡,将 R 0 降低到 1 以下可能无法消除 猴痘。基于 DRC 的 暴发 数据的数值结果表明: (1)人际接触增加有可能使疾病恶化,(2)高隔离率和感染个体的加速康复通过任何可能的干预可以轻松遏制疾病。结果进一步表明,环境污染并没有显着影响疾病 传播 的发病率。更重要的是,据观察,实施有影响力的缓解措施会导致感染人数的峰值降低和延迟。这对于医疗保健系统在最需要时为更多紧急情况和隔离设施做好准备至关重要,特别是在资源匮乏的社区或国家。我们的研究结果强调需要针对行为和环境因素采取综合干预措施,特别是在资源有限的环境中。

full_text: Nature Reviews Microbiology nature reviews microbiology https://doi.org/10.1038/s41579-026-01372-1 Review article Check for updates Towards broader-spectrum direct-acting antivirals against RNA viruses Hendrik Jan Thibaut 1, Dirk Jochmans 1,3, Christophe Van Dijck2,3, Manon Laporte 1,3, Laurens Liesenborghs 2 & Johan Neyts1 Abstract Small molecule antiviral drugs have transformed the management of infections such as those caused by HIV, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, herpesviruses and influenza viruses. Effective antiviral therapeutics remain unavailable for many other often life-threatening viral infections, many of which are caused by RNA viruses. The development of potent, safe and orally available antivirals is therefore essential both to address current unmet medical needs and to strengthen epidemic and pandemic preparedness. In this Review, we discuss the rationale for building a diversified portfolio of broader-spectrum antivirals against RNA viruses with activity spanning multiple genera, entire families or even crossing viral families. We provide a non-exhaustive overview of approved and investigational antiviral agents active against RNA viruses and discuss the biological determinants that underlie their antiviral spectrum. Finally, we outline the clinical development frameworks required to accelerate the evaluation of such drugs, in particular in the context of outbreaks. Sections Introduction One drug to treat them all? Direct-acting antivirals versus host-targeting antivirals New approaches to discover new targets for broader-acting antivirals Translational readiness Conclusions 1KU Leuven Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Transplantation, Antiviral Drug and Vaccine Research Group, Leuven, Belgium. 2Department of Clinical Sciences, Institute of Tropical Medicine, Antwerp, Belgium. 3These authors contributed equally: Dirk Jochmans, Christophe Van Dijck, Manon Laporte. e-mail: johan.neyts@kuleuven.be Nature Reviews Microbiology Review article Alongside vaccine development, sustained investment in antiviral drug discovery is therefore essential. Antiviral drug development has so far largely been focused on viral infections that offer large and predict- able commercial markets (for example, those caused by HIV and HCV). It is obviously unrealistic and economically unsustainable to develop specific antiviral drugs for each known viral pathogen. Newly emerging viruses will most likely belong to viral families already known (Table 1) today. Advances in metagenomics and high-throughput sequencing greatly expanded our understanding of viral diversity, and although new viral families may still be discovered, such events are becoming increasingly rare. Together, this strongly supports a strategy in which broader-acting small molecule antiviral (BSA) drugs are developed. Such drugs can be used for the treatment and prophylaxis of infec- tions with known viruses for which no antiviral treatment is available and, in the case of epidemics or pandemics, as a rapid response option while other countermeasures, such as vaccines and mAbs, are being developed12,13. In this Review, we discuss the rationale for the development of BSAs and provide a non-exhaustive overview of approved or experi- mental antiviral drugs active against viruses with an RNA genome. We also outline strategies for target discovery and accelerated clinical development. One drug to treat them all? The term ‘broad-spectrum’ antiviral has been widely used but lacks, to the best of our knowledge, a clear definition. Here, we propose instead to use the term ‘broader-spectrum’ antivirals and distinguish three categories: (i) cross-family BSAs with activity across unrelated viral families within or across a certain genome architecture, that is, negative-sense single-stranded RNA ((−)ssRNA), positive-sense single-stranded RNA ((+)ssRNA) or double-stranded RNA (dsRNA); (ii) pan-family BSAs that act across the different genera of a given viral family (for example, pan-paramyxovirus drugs); and (iii) intra-family BSAs, which are active against multiple serotypes and genotypes of a particular virus (for example, pan-serotype dengue virus (DENV) Introduction Viruses, whether known or yet to emerge (‘virus X’), remain a major threat to global health. Vaccines, monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) and antiviral drugs are each important and complementary in controlling viral infections. Vaccination has led to the eradication of smallpox, brought polio close to eradication and massively reduced disease and mortality associated with numerous viral infections, such as measles virus, mumps virus, rubella virus, influenza virus, severe acute respira- tory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), hepatitis B virus (HBV) and human papillomavirus1–3. For several important human pathogens, such as HIV, hepatitis C virus (HCV), herpes simplex viruses (HSV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), rhinoviruses and many others, the devel- opment of highly effective vaccines has proved difficult or remains elusive, often despite decades of intensive effort. Therefore, it cannot be guaranteed that efficacious vaccines can always be developed when new threatening viruses emerge4,5. mAbs can offer immediate protection and are transforming the prophylaxis or treatment of certain acute viral diseases, such as those caused by the rabies virus6 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)7. They generally have an excellent safety profile and can be highly effective, although they require injections, are virus specific or variant spe- cific and can rapidly select for escape variants8,9. Like vaccines, mAbs can be developed only once a new pathogen has been identified and characterized. By contrast, small molecule antiviral drugs offer several distinct advantages. They can be administered orally and have the potential to cover a broader spectrum of viruses (Box 1) than vaccines and mAbs. Antiviral drugs have revolutionized the treatment of certain (chronic) viral infections such as those caused by either HIV, HBV, HCV, HSV-1 and HSV-2, and CMV. More recently, antiviral drugs have also become availa- ble against some other viruses including influenza viruses, SARS-CoV-2 and hepatitis delta virus. However, for the majority of the more than 200 known human pathogenic viruses, no antiviral drugs are available. Most of these viruses are RNA viruses — the focus of this Review — including many emerging and clinically important pathogens10–12. Box 1 | Categories and examples of broader-spectrum antivirals (BSAs) for RNA viruses Cross-family BSAs Active against viruses belonging to different (related or unrelated) viral families or across a certain genome architecture (that is, negative-sense single-stranded RNA ((−)ssRNA), positive-sense single-stranded RNA ((+)ssRNA) or double-stranded RNA (dsRNA viruses)), typically by targeting conserved features of the viral replication machinery such as the catalytic site of viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerases. For example, remdesivir, a nucleoside viral polymerase inhibitor, is active against viruses belonging to different viral families, that is, the (−)ssRNA Filoviridae, Paramyxoviridae, Pneumoviridae and Arenaviridae as well as the (+) ssRNA Flaviviridae, Picornaviridae and Coronaviridae. Baloxavir, an endonuclease inhibitor, inhibits influenza A and B viruses (family Orthomyxoviridae) but also, although much less potently, several members of the family Peribunyaviridae. Pan-family BSAs Active across all or at least most genera within a single viral family. Examples include neuraminidase inhibitors such as oseltamivir, zanamivir and peramivir that are active against both influenza A and B viruses (family Orthomyxoviridae). Nirmatrelvir is a reversible covalent, peptidomimetic Mpro inhibitor that inhibits human and animal coronaviruses belonging to different genera within the family Coronaviridae. Intra-family BSAs Can be active against multiple serotypes, genotypes or strains of a particular virus species. For example, mosnodenvir is active against all dengue virus genotypes (family Flaviviridae) by blocking the interaction between viral proteins NS4B and NS3. Intra-family broader-spectrum activity may span several viruses within one genus of a particular family without extending to other genera. For example, the non-covalent, non-peptidomimetic Mpro inhibitor ensitrelvir is active only against members of the genus Betacoronavirus (severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), SARS-CoV-1 and human coronavirus (HCoV)-OC43), but not against members of the genus Alphacoronavirus (such as HCoV-229E and HCoV-NL63) within the family Coronaviridae. Nature Reviews Microbiology Review article inhibitors) or active against one or more (but not all) genera of a viral family (Box 1). The need for broader-acting antivirals and their desired spectrum of activity are mostly defined by the particular (clinical) context (Boxes 2 and 3). For viruses that cause a high number of annual cases (for example, RSV), there might be a sufficiently large market, and thus incentives, to develop virus-specific drugs. Conversely, there might be no or less financial incentive to develop virus-specific drugs for viruses that cause a rather limited number of cases but that col- lectively, within their genus or family, are responsible for a substan- tial clinical burden (for example, coxsackieviruses and echoviruses, EV-D68 and EV-A71 that all belong to the genus Enterovirus). In this case, the development of antivirals that are broadly active across the entire Enterovirus genus (pan-Enterovirus; category intra-family BSAs) represents a more realistic approach. In the context of epidemic or pan- demic preparedness, access to pan-family and cross-family BSAs may be particularly important, as it cannot be predicted which viral family a newly emerging pathogen (‘virus X’) will belong to. Given the extensive genetic diversity and distinct replication strategies of viral families, the development of a single cross-family drug with potent activity against all RNA virus families is likely to be unrealistic. Rather, a more feasible strategy may be to establish a portfolio of different types of BSAs that collectively provide, either alone or in combination, coverage across the RNA virus landscape. BSAs may also be valuable in the context of viral co-infections, in which a single drug could simultaneously target two (or more) viruses14,15. Beyond the spectrum of activity, BSA development must be guided by clearly defined target product profiles16. To have a meaningful clinical impact, BSAs (or combinations thereof) should ideally be highly efficacious, be orally available (preferably once daily dosing), be safe for a broad patient population (preferably including pregnant women and children), possess a (relatively) high barrier to resistance and exhibit minimal drug–drug interactions16. Virus tissue tropism further influences desirable drug properties. For example, infections involving the central nervous system require efficient blood–brain barrier penetration, whereas limited penetration may be preferable for peripheral viral infections. Consequently, distinct target product profiles may be required, even within a single viral genus. The importance of preparedness against known viruses (such as EV-D6818, Ebola virus19, monkeypox virus20 and Andes hantavirus21) as well as against emerging viral threats (for example, SARS-CoV-2) has been repeatedly illustrated during outbreaks caused by these diverse viral pathogens. During the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19 pan- demic), no antiviral drugs were available at the onset. A stockpile of an oral, pan-family coronavirus BSA before the start of the COVID-19 pan- demic would likely have saved countless lives22,23. Remdesivir, originally discovered as an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) inhibitor of RSV24 and Ebola viruses25,26, was the only drug for which antiviral activity against coronaviruses had been systematically demonstrated in preclinical models before the pandemic27. In the absence of readily available and effective antiviral treat- ments, drug repurposing may need to be considered. Repurpos- ing can provide a rapid and relatively cost-effective response by leveraging de-risked drugs with existing preclinical and clinical safety data28,29. However, drugs developed or used for non-viral indi- cations are mostly unlikely to possess sufficient antiviral potency to curb outbreaks caused by newly emerging and (potentially highly) pathogenic viruses. At the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, extensive repurposing initiatives studied whether drugs approved for other indications could inhibit SARS-CoV-2 replication. Drugs such as azithro- mycin (antibiotic), itraconazole (antifungal), hydroxychloroquine (antimalarial, antirheumatic), niclosamide (anthelmintic), ivermectin (anthelmintic) and nitazoxanide (antiparasitic) rapidly entered numer- ous clinical trials, many of them small and underpowered, and even became, for some time, standard treatment in certain settings despite limited preclinical evidence30. Overall, drug repurposing efforts dur- ing the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic were largely unsuccessful, highlighting that such strategies should not be initiated only at the time a new virus emerges. A more realistic approach is to systematically assess existing drugs during epidemic or pandemic ‘peace-time’ against panels of viruses that are representative of high-risk families. Drugs with ‘reason- able’ in vitro activity can be further tested, alone or in combinations, in preclinical models13. Studies in SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters revealed that combi- nations of two or three antivirals, each used at suboptimal or even inactive doses, can result in important antiviral effects31. To ration- ally develop combination strategies for BSAs, systematic preclinical testing of combinations across viral families is required. Extensive preclinical studies of the most promising combinations may help to guide strategies for stockpiling for epidemic or pandemic prepared- ness. full_text_sections.full_text: Nature Reviews Microbiology nature reviews microbiology https://doi.org/10.1038/s41579-026-01372-1 Review article Check for updates Towards broader-spectrum direct-acting antivirals against RNA viruses Hendrik Jan Thibaut 1, Dirk Jochmans 1,3, Christophe Van Dijck2,3, Manon Laporte 1,3, Laurens Liesenborghs 2 & Johan Neyts1 Abstract Small molecule antiviral drugs have transformed the management of infections such as those caused by HIV, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, herpesviruses and influenza viruses. Effective antiviral therapeutics remain unavailable for many other often life-threatening viral infections, many of which are caused by RNA viruses. The development of potent, safe and orally available antivirals is therefore essential both to address current unmet medical needs and to strengthen epidemic and pandemic preparedness. In this Review, we discuss the rationale for building a diversified portfolio of broader-spectrum antivirals against RNA viruses with activity spanning multiple genera, entire families or even crossing viral families. We provide a non-exhaustive overview of approved and investigational antiviral agents active against RNA viruses and discuss the biological determinants that underlie their antiviral spectrum. Finally, we outline the clinical development frameworks required to accelerate the evaluation of such drugs, in particular in the context of outbreaks. Sections Introduction One drug to treat them all? Direct-acting antivirals versus host-targeting antivirals New approaches to discover new targets for broader-acting antivirals Translational readiness Conclusions 1KU Leuven Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Transplantation, Antiviral Drug and Vaccine Research Group, Leuven, Belgium. 2Department of Clinical Sciences, Institute of Tropical Medicine, Antwerp, Belgium. 3These authors contributed equally: Dirk Jochmans, Christophe Van Dijck, Manon Laporte. e-mail: johan.neyts@kuleuven.be Nature Reviews Microbiology Review article Alongside vaccine development, sustained investment in antiviral drug discovery is therefore essential. Antiviral drug development has so far largely been focused on viral infections that offer large and predict- able commercial markets (for example, those caused by HIV and HCV). It is obviously unrealistic and economically unsustainable to develop specific antiviral drugs for each known viral pathogen. Newly emerging viruses will most likely belong to viral families already known (Table 1) today. Advances in metagenomics and high-throughput sequencing greatly expanded our understanding of viral diversity, and although new viral families may still be discovered, such events are becoming increasingly rare. Together, this strongly supports a strategy in which broader-acting small molecule antiviral (BSA) drugs are developed. Such drugs can be used for the treatment and prophylaxis of infec- tions with known viruses for which no antiviral treatment is available and, in the case of epidemics or pandemics, as a rapid response option while other countermeasures, such as vaccines and mAbs, are being developed12,13. In this Review, we discuss the rationale for the development of BSAs and provide a non-exhaustive overview of approved or experi- mental antiviral drugs active against viruses with an RNA genome. We also outline strategies for target discovery and accelerated clinical development. One drug to treat them all? The term ‘broad-spectrum’ antiviral has been widely used but lacks, to the best of our knowledge, a clear definition. Here, we propose instead to use the term ‘broader-spectrum’ antivirals and distinguish three categories: (i) cross-family BSAs with activity across unrelated viral families within or across a certain genome architecture, that is, negative-sense single-stranded RNA ((−)ssRNA), positive-sense single-stranded RNA ((+)ssRNA) or double-stranded RNA (dsRNA); (ii) pan-family BSAs that act across the different genera of a given viral family (for example, pan-paramyxovirus drugs); and (iii) intra-family BSAs, which are active against multiple serotypes and genotypes of a particular virus (for example, pan-serotype dengue virus (DENV) Introduction Viruses, whether known or yet to emerge (‘virus X’), remain a major threat to global health. Vaccines, monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) and antiviral drugs are each important and complementary in controlling viral infections. Vaccination has led to the eradication of smallpox, brought polio close to eradication and massively reduced disease and mortality associated with numerous viral infections, such as measles virus, mumps virus, rubella virus, influenza virus, severe acute respira- tory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), hepatitis B virus (HBV) and human papillomavirus1–3. For several important human pathogens, such as HIV, hepatitis C virus (HCV), herpes simplex viruses (HSV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), rhinoviruses and many others, the devel- opment of highly effective vaccines has proved difficult or remains elusive, often despite decades of intensive effort. Therefore, it cannot be guaranteed that efficacious vaccines can always be developed when new threatening viruses emerge4,5. mAbs can offer immediate protection and are transforming the prophylaxis or treatment of certain acute viral diseases, such as those caused by the rabies virus6 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)7. They generally have an excellent safety profile and can be highly effective, although they require injections, are virus specific or variant spe- cific and can rapidly select for escape variants8,9. Like vaccines, mAbs can be developed only once a new pathogen has been identified and characterized. By contrast, small molecule antiviral drugs offer several distinct advantages. They can be administered orally and have the potential to cover a broader spectrum of viruses (Box 1) than vaccines and mAbs. Antiviral drugs have revolutionized the treatment of certain (chronic) viral infections such as those caused by either HIV, HBV, HCV, HSV-1 and HSV-2, and CMV. More recently, antiviral drugs have also become availa- ble against some other viruses including influenza viruses, SARS-CoV-2 and hepatitis delta virus. However, for the majority of the more than 200 known human pathogenic viruses, no antiviral drugs are available. Most of these viruses are RNA viruses — the focus of this Review — including many emerging and clinically important pathogens10–12. Box 1 | Categories and examples of broader-spectrum antivirals (BSAs) for RNA viruses Cross-family BSAs Active against viruses belonging to different (related or unrelated) viral families or across a certain genome architecture (that is, negative-sense single-stranded RNA ((−)ssRNA), positive-sense single-stranded RNA ((+)ssRNA) or double-stranded RNA (dsRNA viruses)), typically by targeting conserved features of the viral replication machinery such as the catalytic site of viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerases. For example, remdesivir, a nucleoside viral polymerase inhibitor, is active against viruses belonging to different viral families, that is, the (−)ssRNA Filoviridae, Paramyxoviridae, Pneumoviridae and Arenaviridae as well as the (+) ssRNA Flaviviridae, Picornaviridae and Coronaviridae. Baloxavir, an endonuclease inhibitor, inhibits influenza A and B viruses (family Orthomyxoviridae) but also, although much less potently, several members of the family Peribunyaviridae. Pan-family BSAs Active across all or at least most genera within a single viral family. Examples include neuraminidase inhibitors such as oseltamivir, zanamivir and peramivir that are active against both influenza A and B viruses (family Orthomyxoviridae). title_original: Towards broader-spectrum direct-acting antivirals against RNA viruses

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on the development of broader-spectrum direct-acting antivirals (BSAs) against RNA viruses, with a particular emphasis on the monkeypox virus (MPXV) and its clades. The central question is how to create antivirals that can target multiple RNA viruses, including MPXV, across different viral families and genera.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a systematic analysis of antiviral drug development, drawing on advances in metagenomics and high-throughput sequencing to understand viral diversity. It discusses the rationale for developing BSAs, provides an overview of approved and experimental antiviral agents, and outlines clinical development frameworks for evaluating such drugs, particularly in outbreak scenarios.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that the development of BSAs is essential to address current unmet medical needs and to strengthen epidemic and pandemic preparedness. It highlights the importance of broad-spectrum antivirals in the context of emerging viral threats, such as SARS-CoV-2, and emphasizes the need for a diversified portfolio of antivirals against RNA viruses.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review notes that the term 'broad-spectrum' antiviral lacks a clear definition and proposes the use of 'broader-spectrum' instead. It also highlights the limitations of some antiviral drugs, such as azithromycin and hydroxychloroquine, which were used in clinical trials with limited preclinical evidence. Additionally, it points out that the development of BSAs is still in its early stages and requires further research.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review suggests that fixed-dose combinations of antivirals, similar to those used in HIV treatment, could be ideal for combating multiple RNA viruses. It also emphasizes the importance of investing in antiviral drug discovery for both known and emerging viral threats, including MPXV, to improve preparedness and response capabilities.

analysis.summary_en: This review discusses the development of broader-spectrum direct-acting antivirals (BSAs) against RNA viruses, including the monkeypox virus (MPXV). It highlights the need for such drugs to address current unmet medical needs and enhance pandemic preparedness. The review outlines the rationale for BSAs, their potential applications in treating and preventing viral infections, and the challenges in defining and developing these agents. It also emphasizes the importance of fixed-dose combinations and sustained investment in antiviral research. The review notes that while some antivirals have shown promise, their efficacy and safety remain uncertain, underscoring the need for further studies and improved clinical frameworks.

analysis_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 本评论文章得出结论,开发BSAs对于应对当前未满足的医疗需求和加强流行病和大流行病的应对能力至关重要。它强调了在面对如SARS-CoV-2等新兴病毒威胁时,广谱抗病毒药物药物的重要性,并强调了针对RNA病毒开发多样化抗病毒药物药物的必要性。
analysis_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 本评论文章指出,'广谱' 抗病毒药物这一术语缺乏明确的定义,并建议使用'更广谱'一词。它还强调了一些抗病毒药物药物的局限性,例如阿奇霉素和羟氯喹,这些药物在临床试验中使用时缺乏充分的临床前证据。此外,它指出BSAs的开发仍处于早期阶段,需要进一步研究。
analysis_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 本评论文章建议,类似于HIV 治疗中使用的固定剂量组合,针对多种RNA病毒的抗病毒药物固定剂量组合可能是理想的解决方案。它还强调了对已知和新兴病毒威胁(包括MPXV)进行抗病毒药物药物发现投资的重要性,以提高应对和响应能力。

title: Quarantine-associated viral pathogens in non-human primates: pathobiology, diagnostic surveillance, control strategies, and one health implications

source_records.title: Quarantine-associated viral pathogens in non-human primates: pathobiology, diagnostic surveillance, control strategies, and one health implications

priority_tier_reason: 补充性记录、预印本或证据完整度有限
full_text: Recent outbreaks of emerging infectious diseases, along with advances in neurological and other biomedical research, have increased the use of non-human primates (NHPs) as preclinical models. Their close phylogenetic and physiological similarities to humans make them valuable for translational research, especially during public health emergencies. However, NHPs can harbor a wide range of viral pathogens, some of which pose zoonotic risks and may compromise animal health and experimental reproducibility. Therefore, quarantine procedures, pathogen surveillance, and biosecurity programs are essential for the safe and reliable use of NHPs in research. Despite this need, comprehensive reviews linking national quarantine policies with the biological and epidemiological characteristics of major viral pathogens and their relevance to disease surveillance and control remain limited. This review compares national quarantine frameworks for NHPs, examines pathogen-specific features, and discusses their implications for quarantine and surveillance. We emphasize the need for an integrated, risk-based approach incorporating longitudinal microbiological monitoring, multimodal diagnostic assessment, facility-level response procedures, occupational health preparedness, and internationally harmonized quarantine standards. 4DiscussionRecent WHO pathogen prioritization efforts have emphasized family-level preparedness and response strategies (197). This concept is also relevant to NHP quarantine because many viruses of concern in primate colonies, particularly members of the families Retroviridae and Herpesviridae, are capable of establishing persistent or latent infections (Table 2). In addition, other important pathogens, such as polyomaviruses and mycobacteria, may persist chronically after introduction. These biological features make complete elimination difficult. Moreover, NHP breeding and research facilities often rely on long-term group-housing systems, which may facilitate pathogen maintenance and transmission within colonies. Given that major NHP-associated viruses can be transmitted through horizontal and, in some cases, vertical routes, the introduction of infected animals may increase the likelihood of transmission to other animals within the colony (Table 3). microbiological monitoring because many NHP-associated viruses generally cause asymptomatic or only mild infections, although various clinical manifestations may occasionally occur (Figure 2). Nevertheless, microbiological surveillance standards differ among countries, and enforceable requirements remain limited. Given that NHPs are commonly distributed from a limited number of breeding facilities to research institutions worldwide, effective quarantine should be addressed not only at the level of individual facilities but also harmonized international standards and coordinated surveillance (18). From a One Health perspective, there is a need to define a minimum set of diseases for quarantine screening, particularly latent or persistent viral infections and tuberculosis, to reduce the risks associated with the international movement of NHPs. Their potential for subclinical infection and zoonotic transmission further highlights the importance of integrated surveillance for NHP colony health, occupational safety, research reliability, and public health (Figure 3). However, important knowledge gaps remain regarding transmission dynamics in NHP research and facility settings and the associated risks to humans. The current evidence base is also limited by uneven species coverage, heterogeneity among institutions and surveillance practices, and insufficient data for certain viral pathogens. Given these uncertainties, a precautionary approach based on a minimum level of routine surveillance is warranted to reduce the risk of undetected infection and transmission. Considering the variability in screening practices among institutions and the limitations of direct antigen or pathogen detection for many retroviruses and herpesviruses, we propose that this minimum surveillance framework should include at least annual antibody testing for major persistent or latent viruses, including SIV, SRV, STLV, B virus, SCMV, and SVV.Figure 2Differential diagnostic overview of quarantine-associated major viral diseases in non-human primates by clinical presentation and host group. Among macaque viruses, B virus, SIV, STLV, and SV40 can infect humans; B virus, STLV, and SV40 are associated with subclinical or persistent infection in nonhuman primates, while B virus is highlighted as potentially fatal in humans.In addition to determining seropositivity using established diagnostic cut-off values, longitudinal evaluation of antibody titers, rather than reliance on a single time-point measurement, may be important for assessing infection status and identifying changes associated with exposure, viral reactivation, or potential transmission within a colony. Antibody results should also be evaluated beyond the individual animal level, with comparisons among groups, housing rooms, and facilities to identify temporal changes in exposure and transmission patterns. Nevertheless, antibody testing should not be used in isolation. Serological findings should be interpreted together with clinical observation, necropsy findings, antigen or molecular assays, hematological and serum biochemical data, and expert interpretation. Because infected animals may exhibit only mild or no apparent clinical signs and viral shedding may be intermittent, repeated antigen or molecular testing of animals with suspected infection or positive serological findings may be necessary to confirm active viral shedding.Furthermore, facility-level standard operating procedures (SOPs) should be established in advance for each pathogen to define appropriate response measures according to different combinations of diagnostic results, such as seropositivity alone or concurrent positive serological and antigen or molecular findings. The detection of these pathogens should prompt the implementation of appropriate SOPs to prevent further transmission within the colony, restrict the transfer of infected or exposed animals, and protect personnel from zoonotic exposure. For high-risk zoonotic agents such as B virus, rapid post-exposure evaluation and appropriate antiviral prophylaxis or treatment are particularly important to reduce the risk of severe human disease. Thus, SOPs, routine training, exposure-response plans, and access to appropriate medical countermeasures should be established before incidents occur.In addition to viruses of the families Retroviridae and Herpesviridae, four viral diseases of particular concern were also included because of their high pathogenicity in humans and recent public health importance. Although NHPs are not generally considered natural reservoirs for these viruses, they may become infected as susceptible or incidental hosts and therefore warrant consideration during quarantine. Because these infections can cause recognizable clinical signs in macaques, as in humans, careful clinical surveillance is important during the quarantine period. Unlike persistent or latent viral infections, quarantine surveillance for Marburg virus, Ebola virus, MPXV, and rabies virus should focus on the early recognition of suggestive clinical signs, followed by the implementation of appropriate precautionary biosafety measures before prompt diagnostic testing using antigen or molecular assays and, when necessary, postmortem examination. Rapid identification of suspected or confirmed cases should then trigger appropriate public health and facility-level response measures, including assessment and management of potentially exposed personnel, isolation of affected animals, and measures to prevent further transmission. 1IntroductionZoonotic infectious diseases are increasingly emerging worldwide, driven by multiple factors, including increased global travel and trade, climate change, urbanization, and land-use change (1). In recent years, viruses with pandemic potential, such as severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) and highly pathogenic avian influenza viruses (HPAIVs), have posed significant global public health threats. In response to these emerging infectious diseases, various preclinical animal models have been widely used in infectious disease researches, including mice, hamsters, ferrets, guinea pigs, and non-human primates (NHPs) (2). Because effective therapeutics and vaccines may not be readily available for newly emerging viral diseases, preclinical studies using animal models play an important role in the development and evaluation of novel countermeasures.NHP models are more anatomically, physiologically, immunologically, and genetically similar to humans than other commonly used preclinical animal models. For this reason, NHPs have often been used as important preclinical models to investigate the pathogenesis of infections, caused by Ebola virus, SARS-CoV-2, and H5N1 HPAIVs and to support the development of vaccines and therapeutics against these viruses (3–6). For example, mRNA vaccines targeting SARS-CoV-2 have been evaluated for efficacy and safety using NHP models. In addition, ZMapp, a monoclonal antibody-based therapy against Ebola virus, demonstrated efficacy in treating Ebola virus infection in NHP models (7). These findings from NHP studies provided evidence supporting the clinical translation and emergency use of these interventions during outbreaks under regulatory and ethical frameworks such as the WHO MEURI guidelines (8). Consequently, the use of NHP models has increased significantly in recent years, resulting in a shortage of available NHPs (9, 10).NHPs have been reported globally to harbor various pathogens that can cause latent or subclinical infections, including B virus (Cercopithecine herpesvirus 1), simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), simian T cell lymphotropic/leukemia virus (STLV), simian type D retrovirus (SRV), and Mycobacterium (M) tuberculosis, all of which should be absent from specific pathogen-free (SPF) colonies (11–13) (Figure 1). Also, simian polyomaviruses, including simian virus 40 (SV40), have been detected macaque species (14). Therefore, latent or subclinical infections in clinically healthy NHPs may compromise the reproducibility of experimental outcomes and pose a risk of zoonotic transmission to laboratory personnel. Potentially lethal zoonotic viruses, including rabies virus, Marburg virus, Ebola virus, monkeypox virus, and yellow fever virus, have been reported in NHP species (15).Figure 1Global distribution of documented viral infections and outbreaks in non-human primates. full_text_sections.abstract: Recent outbreaks of emerging infectious diseases, along with advances in neurological and other biomedical research, have increased the use of non-human primates (NHPs) as preclinical models. Their close phylogenetic and physiological similarities to humans make them valuable for translational research, especially during public health emergencies. However, NHPs can harbor a wide range of viral pathogens, some of which pose zoonotic risks and may compromise animal health and experimental reproducibility. Therefore, quarantine procedures, pathogen surveillance, and biosecurity programs are essential for the safe and reliable use of NHPs in research. Despite this need, comprehensive reviews linking national quarantine policies with the biological and epidemiological characteristics of major viral pathogens and their relevance to disease surveillance and control remain limited. This review compares national quarantine frameworks for NHPs, examines pathogen-specific features, and discusses their implications for quarantine and surveillance. We emphasize the need for an integrated, risk-based approach incorporating longitudinal microbiological monitoring, multimodal diagnostic assessment, facility-level response procedures, occupational health preparedness, and internationally harmonized quarantine standards.
full_text_sections.discussion: 4DiscussionRecent WHO pathogen prioritization efforts have emphasized family-level preparedness and response strategies (197). This concept is also relevant to NHP quarantine because many viruses of concern in primate colonies, particularly members of the families Retroviridae and Herpesviridae, are capable of establishing persistent or latent infections (Table 2). In addition, other important pathogens, such as polyomaviruses and mycobacteria, may persist chronically after introduction. These biological features make complete elimination difficult. Moreover, NHP breeding and research facilities often rely on long-term group-housing systems, which may facilitate pathogen maintenance and transmission within colonies. Given that major NHP-associated viruses can be transmitted through horizontal and, in some cases, vertical routes, the introduction of infected animals may increase the likelihood of transmission to other animals within the colony (Table 3). full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionZoonotic infectious diseases are increasingly emerging worldwide, driven by multiple factors, including increased global travel and trade, climate change, urbanization, and land-use change (1). In recent years, viruses with pandemic potential, such as severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) and highly pathogenic avian influenza viruses (HPAIVs), have posed significant global public health threats. In response to these emerging infectious diseases, various preclinical animal models have been widely used in infectious disease researches, including mice, hamsters, ferrets, guinea pigs, and non-human primates (NHPs) (2). Because effective therapeutics and vaccines may not be readily available for newly emerging viral diseases, preclinical studies using animal models play an important role in the development and evaluation of novel countermeasures.NHP models are more anatomically, physiologically, immunologically, and genetically similar to humans than other commonly used preclinical animal models. For this reason, NHPs have often been used as important preclinical models to investigate the pathogenesis of infections, caused by Ebola virus, SARS-CoV-2, and H5N1 HPAIVs and to support the development of vaccines and therapeutics against these viruses (3–6). For example, mRNA vaccines targeting SARS-CoV-2 have been evaluated for efficacy and safety using NHP models. In addition, ZMapp, a monoclonal antibody-based therapy against Ebola virus, demonstrated efficacy in treating Ebola virus infection in NHP models (7). These findings from NHP studies provided evidence supporting the clinical translation and emergency use of these interventions during outbreaks under regulatory and ethical frameworks such as the WHO MEURI guidelines (8). Consequently, the use of NHP models has increased significantly in recent years, resulting in a shortage of available NHPs (9, 10).NHPs have been reported globally to harbor various pathogens that can cause latent or subclinical infections, including B virus (Cercopithecine herpesvirus 1), simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), simian T cell lymphotropic/leukemia virus (STLV), simian type D retrovirus (SRV), and Mycobacterium (M) tuberculosis, all of which should be absent from specific pathogen-free (SPF) colonies (11–13) (Figure 1). Also, simian polyomaviruses, including simian virus 40 (SV40), have been detected macaque species (14). Therefore, latent or subclinical infections in clinically healthy NHPs may compromise the reproducibility of experimental outcomes and pose a risk of zoonotic transmission to laboratory personnel. Potentially lethal zoonotic viruses, including rabies virus, Marburg virus, Ebola virus, monkeypox virus, and yellow fever virus, have been reported in NHP species (15).Figure 1Global distribution of documented viral infections and outbreaks in non-human primates. This heterogeneity may lead to individual variation in susceptibility to infectious agents. Outdoor housing and husbandry practices can further hinder the establishment and maintenance of SPF colonies (17). Therefore, appropriate quarantine procedures are essential for NHPs. This review provides an overview of national quarantine protocols and major viral pathogens relevant to NHPs. We focus on pathogen biology and epidemiology, diagnostic approaches, and interventions, and consider their implications for risk-based quarantine, surveillance, and infection-control strategies. We also highlight the need for coordinated facility-level responses, occupational health preparedness, and internationally harmonized quarantine standards from a One Health perspective. 2International quarantine policies and virus surveillance in NHPs facilities2.1Republic of KoreaIn the Republic of Korea, the importation of NHPs is regulated under the Act on the Prevention of Contagious Animal Diseases, and these species are classified as designated quarantine animals subject to mandatory veterinary inspection upon importation. Experimental macaques, primarily cynomolgus (Macaca fascicularis) and rhesus (Macaca mulatta) macaques, are predominantly imported from Asian countries, including China, Vietnam, and Cambodia (10, 18). Imported NHPs must undergo at least 30 days of pre-export quarantine under the supervision of a government-designated veterinarian in the exporting country, followed by an additional 30-day quarantine at a designated national animal quarantine facility in Korea prior to release for research use. Specific sanitary import requirements are defined in the national import health regulations for NHP species (19). These regulations require that the exporting country be free from Ebola virus and Marburg virus diseases. The breeding facility of origin must have no evidence of clinical, serological, or pathological occurrence of measles, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, monkeypox, or tuberculosis (M. tuberculosis and M. bovis) for at least 24 months prior to export. During the mandatory pre-export quarantine period, NHPs must be confirmed negative for tuberculosis, internal and external parasites, and enteric bacterial pathogens, including Salmonella spp., Shigella spp., and Yersinia spp. Tuberculosis screening must include at least one tuberculin skin test (TST) conducted within one week after the start of quarantine, while hepatitis B virus testing is additionally required for gibbons and great apes.Beyond these national regulatory mandates, research institutions often conduct additional microbiological screening. However, the pathogens targeted for screening vary according to facility policies, research objectives, and biosafety requirements. Additional screening may include testing for B virus, SIV, STLV, SRV, and other facility-specific pathogens.2.2United statesIn the United States, the importation of NHPs is regulated by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) under the Public Health Service Act (20). All imported NHPs must undergo quarantine for a minimum of 31 days in a CDC-registered facility prior to release. At the federal regulatory level, tuberculosis surveillance via serial TST is the only routine laboratory test universally required during quarantine. Each NHP must receive at least three TSTs administered on the eyelid using mammalian old tuberculin (MOT), at intervals of at least 2 weeks. Reactions must be evaluated at 24, 48, and 72 h after each test. Routine laboratory screening for other diseases is not uniformly required, although additional diagnostic testing may be required under specific clinical circumstances, including filovirus testing in Old World NHPs exhibiting clinical signs suggestive of filovirus disease.Beyond federal requirements, individual research institutions may implement additional quarantine measures based on their own policies. For example, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) requires documentation of a negative TST within 30 days prior to shipment (21). analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the need for improved quarantine and surveillance practices for non-human primates (NHPs) due to their role in preclinical research and the zoonotic risks they pose. The background highlights the increasing use of NHPs in research and the associated risks of viral pathogens.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a review comparing national quarantine frameworks for NHPs, examining pathogen-specific features, and discussing their implications for quarantine and surveillance. It focuses on the biological and epidemiological characteristics of major viral pathogens relevant to disease surveillance and control in NHPs.
analysis.methods: The methods involve a comparative analysis of national quarantine policies, pathogen-specific features, and their implications for surveillance and control strategies. The study also considers facility-level responses, occupational health preparedness, and internationally harmonized quarantine standards.
analysis.main_results: The results include the identification of several viral pathogens harbored by NHPs, such as monkeypox virus (MPXV), rabies virus, Marburg virus, Ebola virus, and others. These pathogens are associated with zoonotic risks and can cause clinical manifestations in NHPs similar to those in humans.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that effective quarantine and surveillance are critical for mitigating zoonotic risks and ensuring experimental reproducibility. The novelty lies in the integration of pathogen biology, epidemiology, and international standards to guide risk-based quarantine and infection-control strategies.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the development of integrated, risk-based quarantine and surveillance strategies for NHPs, which are essential for reducing zoonotic transmission risks and ensuring the reliability of preclinical research. They also highlight the importance of coordinated international efforts in managing these pathogens.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence base is limited by uneven species coverage, heterogeneity among institutions and surveillance practices, and insufficient data for certain viral pathogens. These limitations suggest a moderate confidence in the conclusions drawn.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the role of non-human primates (NHPs) in preclinical research and the associated zoonotic risks posed by viral pathogens such as monkeypox virus (MPXV). It highlights the need for improved quarantine and surveillance practices, emphasizing the importance of an integrated, risk-based approach. The review compares national quarantine frameworks, discusses pathogen-specific features, and outlines implications for public health and research. Despite the increasing use of NHPs in research, the evidence base remains limited due to variability in surveillance practices and data availability. The findings suggest that coordinated international efforts and facility-level responses are essential for effective disease control and prevention of zoonotic transmission.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在改善非人灵长类动物(NHPs)的检疫和监测实践,因为它们在临床前研究中的作用以及所带来的人兽共患病风险。背景强调了非人灵长类动物在研究中使用量的增加及其相关的病毒病原体风险。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究是一项综述,比较了非人灵长类动物的国家检疫框架,分析了病原体特异性特征,并讨论了其对检疫和监测的影响。它聚焦于与非人灵长类动物疾病监测和控制相关的重大病毒病原体的生物学和流行病学特征。
elements_zh.methods: 本研究的方法包括对国家检疫政策、病原体特异性特征及其对监测和控制策略的影响进行比较分析。此外,还考虑了机构层面的应对措施、职业健康准备以及国际统一的检疫标准。
elements_zh.main_results: 研究结果包括识别了非人灵长类动物携带的多种病毒病原体,例如猴痘病毒(MPXV)、狂犬病毒、马尔堡病毒、埃博拉病毒等。这些病原体与人兽共患病风险相关,并且在非人灵长类动物中可引起与人类相似的临床表现。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者认为,有效的检疫和监测对于减轻人兽共患病风险和确保实验可重复性至关重要。其创新之处在于将病原体生物学、流行病学以及国际标准整合起来,以指导基于风险的检疫和感染控制策略。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现为非人灵长类动物的整合、基于风险的检疫和监测策略的制定提供了依据,这对于降低人兽共患病风险并确保临床前研究的可靠性至关重要。它们还突显了协调国际努力管理这些病原体的重要性。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 证据基础受到物种覆盖不均、机构间和监测实践的异质性以及某些病毒病原体数据不足的限制。这些局限性表明结论的置信度中等。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在改善非人灵长类动物(NHPs)的检疫和监测实践,因为它们在临床前研究中的作用以及所带来的人兽共患病风险。背景强调了非人灵长类动物在研究中使用量的增加及其相关的病毒病原体风险。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究是一项综述,比较了非人灵长类动物的国家检疫框架,分析了病原体特异性特征,并讨论了其对检疫和监测的影响。它聚焦于与非人灵长类动物疾病监测和控制相关的重大病毒病原体的生物学和流行病学特征。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究的方法包括对国家检疫政策、病原体特异性特征及其对监测和控制策略的影响进行比较分析。此外,还考虑了机构层面的应对措施、职业健康准备以及国际统一的检疫标准。
analysis_zh.main_results: 研究结果包括识别了非人灵长类动物携带的多种病毒病原体,例如猴痘病毒(MPXV)、狂犬病毒、马尔堡病毒、埃博拉病毒等。这些病原体与人兽共患病风险相关,并且在非人灵长类动物中可引起与人类相似的临床表现。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者认为,有效的检疫和监测对于减轻人兽共患病风险和确保实验可重复性至关重要。其创新之处在于将病原体生物学、流行病学以及国际标准整合起来,以指导基于风险的检疫和感染控制策略。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现为非人灵长类动物的整合、基于风险的检疫和监测策略的制定提供了依据,这对于降低人兽共患病风险并确保临床前研究的可靠性至关重要。它们还突显了协调国际努力管理这些病原体的重要性。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 证据基础受到物种覆盖不均、机构间和监测实践的异质性以及某些病毒病原体数据不足的限制。这些局限性表明结论的置信度中等。

title: When the war never ends: conceptual limitations, contextual differences and implications for interventions in continuous traumatic stress in Sub-Saharan Africa
